name: Barbell back squat
rationale: The engine of the whole plan — leg strength that survives mile 80.
cues: Brace before you unrack — big breath into the belt line
Sit down between your hips, chest proud
Drive the whole foot through the floor; knees track over toes
swap_note: Goblet squat if the bar feels off, or box squat to a bench for depth control.

name: Goblet squat
rationale: Warm-up groove and deload option; keeps the torso honest.
cues: Bell tight to the chest, elbows down
Ribs down — do not arch
Full depth, controlled up

name: Romanian deadlift
rationale: Hamstrings and glutes under stretch — descent control for thousands of feet of downhill.
cues: Push the hips back, soft knees, bar shaved down the thighs
Stop where the hamstrings scream, not where the floor is
Flat back is non-negotiable
swap_note: Dumbbell RDL when barbell setup is a faff.

name: Bulgarian split squat
rationale: Single-leg strength with a big stability demand — the closest a gym gets to a rutted trail.
cues: Rear foot laces-down on the bench or the 16in box
Long stance, torso slightly forward loads the glute
Drive through the front heel; wobble is part of the work
kit_note: 16in box gives a better rear-foot height than the bench for most people.
swap_note: Reverse lunge if knees complain; hold the rack for balance while learning.

name: Weighted step-up
rationale: Concentric single-leg power — every stile, every step cut into a fell.
cues: Whole foot on the box, drive without pushing off the back leg
Start at 16in; 18in is the working height; 20in is roughly knee height for you and the hardest
Control the way down — that is half the exercise
kit_note: Plyo box. 16in to learn and for higher reps, 18in as the default, 20in when you want it to bite.
swap_note: Add the weighted vest before you add box height — height changes the joint angles, load does not.

name: Pack step-up (race pack)
rationale: THE mountain-race exercise. Your race pack, loaded, on a box — specificity you cannot buy.
cues: Wear the actual pack you will race with, straps dialled
Start 6 kg, build to race weight +2 kg by end of Phase 2
Steady rhythm, nose-breathing pace — this is durability, not a leg burner
18in box for volume, 20in when you want the big-step demand
kit_note: Race pack + plyo box. Use the pack, not the vest, for this one — the point is rehearsing the exact load carriage you will race under, sway and hip belt included.
swap_note: Vest version if the pack is packed for a race, or stair repeats with the pack on.

name: Single-leg RDL
rationale: Balance + posterior chain + ankle proprioception in one move. Bog insurance.
cues: Kettlebell in the hand opposite the standing leg
Hips square, back leg reaches long
Grip the floor with your toes
swap_note: Hold the rack with the free hand, or B-stance RDL.

name: Lateral lunge
rationale: Frontal-plane strength — the plane running never trains and camber, tussocks and sidesteps punish.
cues: Big sideways step, sit into that hip
Trailing leg straight, both heels down
Push back to standing through the bent leg

name: Kettlebell swing
rationale: Explosive hip power and posterior-chain conditioning in minutes.
cues: It is a hinge, not a squat
Hips throw the bell — arms are just rope
Snap tall at the top, glutes hard

name: Calf raise (slant board)
rationale: Calf capacity is ankle armour and downhill braking. On the slant board the heel drops below the toes, so you get loaded range the floor cannot give you.
cues: 3 s down into the stretch, pause, drive tall
Progress single-leg, then add a dumbbell, then the vest
Full range beats heavy half-reps
kit_note: Slant board. Straight leg targets the gastrocnemius; the bent-knee version below is a separate exercise, not a variation.
swap_note: Off a stair edge if the board is in use.

name: Bent-knee soleus raise
rationale: Bend the knee and the gastrocnemius slackens, so the soleus takes the load. This matters more than most runners realise: the soleus carries the largest single share of force in late-stance running, it is the muscle that quietly fails on long descents, and straight-leg calf raises barely touch it.
cues: Knee bent to about 90°, heel dropped off the board edge
Slow — 2 s up, 3 s down
Load heavy; the soleus tolerates far more than you expect
15–20 reps, and it should burn
kit_note: Slant board plus a dumbbell resting on the knee, or the vest on.
swap_note: Seated on the bench with a dumbbell on the thigh.

name: Tibialis raise
rationale: The shin muscle that lifts your toes over 108 miles of tussock — and guards the ankle.
cues: Lean back on a wall, heels ~30 cm out
Lift both forefeet as high as they go
Slow lowers; burn is the point
kit_note: Reverse the slant board (toes low, heels high) to add range once wall reps get easy.

name: Banded ankle circuit
rationale: Eversion/inversion strength for your ankle history — small muscles, big insurance.
cues: Band around the forefoot: out, in, up — 15 each way
Slow and controlled, seated
Finish with 30 s single-leg balance, eyes closed if easy
swap_note: During toe flare-ups this and isometric holds replace all impact work.

name: Farmer / suitcase carry
rationale: Grip, trunk, posture under load — carrying a heavy pack is literally the sport.
cues: Deadlift the bells up properly
Tall spine, ribs down, brisk short steps
Suitcase (one side) = brutal anti-lean core work
space_note: Needs ~10 m of clear floor. Kept here for when you train outdoors or have the room.
swap_note: No room? Use the suitcase march, front-rack march or shuttle carry below. Marching keeps the stepping rhythm, which matters — see the note on each.

name: Suitcase march (in place)
rationale: The no-space replacement for the suitcase carry. One heavy bell at your side while you march on the spot — the load still tries to fold you sideways, and you still alternate legs, so the anti-lateral-flexion demand arrives in the same rhythm as walking under a pack.
cues: Deadlift the bell up; do not curl it into position
Nose, sternum and belt buckle stacked in a straight line
Knee to hip height, pause a beat, place it down softly
Do not let the free hand grab anything
Swap sides and match the reps exactly
space_note: One square metre. Nothing moves but you.
swap_note: Progress by adding weight before adding time. 45 s a side is plenty; if it gets easy, get a heavier bell.

name: Front-rack march
rationale: Load sits on the front of the ribcage, so the trunk has to resist being pulled into extension while each leg lifts. This is the closest thing in the gym to a heavy chest-mounted pack on a steep climb.
cues: Clean the bells to the shoulders, elbows down and in
Ribs stacked over hips — no arching back
Slow march, full hip height, controlled foot placement
Breathe behind the brace; do not hold your breath
swap_note: Single bell in the rack is harder than two — use it when the double gets easy.

name: Suitcase iso-hold
rationale: Static anti-lean work with a heavier bell than you could march with. Worth knowing that the EMG evidence has holds coming out slightly BELOW the walking versions for trunk activation — so this is the supplement, not the main course. Go heavier and longer to compensate.
cues: Stand tall, shoulders level, load hanging dead straight
Squeeze the opposite glute to stop the hip hiking
Grip is usually what fails first — that is fine, it is trainable
30–45 s a side, heavier than your march weight
swap_note: Barbell version in the rack lets you go much heavier than dumbbells allow.

name: Shuttle carry (5 m turnaround)
rationale: If you can find five metres, this recovers the true walking carry. The turnarounds are a bonus — changing direction under load is exactly what stiles, gates and rocky steps demand.
cues: Short brisk steps, do not stroll
Slow and deliberate on the turn — that is where posture collapses
Set the bells down under control, never drop them
space_note: 5 m each way. Garage, hallway or driveway.
swap_note: Falls back to the suitcase march if five metres is not available.

name: Eccentric box step-down
rationale: The single most descent-specific thing you can do indoors. Running downhill is eccentric work — the quad lengthens under load on every footfall, and when it runs out of capacity you get the shaking, braking, quad-trashed feeling in the back half of a race. This trains exactly that contraction, slowly and under control.
cues: Stand on the box on one leg, other leg hanging free
Lower for a full 4–5 seconds — the slowness IS the exercise
Tap the heel lightly, do not take weight through it
Push back up through the standing leg normally
Knee tracks over the second toe; if it caves inward, drop to a lower box
kit_note: Plyo box. Start 16in, progress to 18in, add the vest before you add height.
ramp_note: Sits on a Saturday, roughly 24 h before your long run — which is the front edge of when eccentric soreness peaks. That is survivable because the dose starts tiny and the repeated bout effect is strong: the first exposure does most of the damage, and by the third or fourth session the same load barely registers. So earn it. Weeks 1–2: one set of four, bodyweight, 16in box. Only add sets, height or vest once a Sunday has passed with no quad stiffness in the first 20 minutes. If a Sunday run ever feels quad-heavy early, drop back a step rather than pushing through.
swap_note: If you would rather not gamble with the long run at all, move it to Tuesday — five days clear, at the cost of stacking quad load on heavy squat day.

name: Pull-up
rationale: The king of upper pulls — back width you can see, grip you can use.
cues: Dead hang start, shoulders down before you pull
Chest to bar direction, not chin-poke
Band assistance or slow negatives until reps come
kit_note: The vest is the cleanest way to load these once you are past ~8 clean reps — far better than a dumbbell between the feet.
swap_note: Band-assisted pull-up or slow 5 s negatives.

name: Overhead press (DB or bar)
rationale: Shoulders that fill a t-shirt and press a pack overhead a fence.
cues: Glutes and core tight — no rib flare
Press to lockout, biceps by ears
Standing beats seated for trunk work

name: Dumbbell bench press
rationale: Chest and triceps with honest, even loading.
cues: Shoulder blades pinned to the bench
Slight arc: down-and-out, up-and-in
Feet planted, leg drive on
swap_note: TRX or deficit push-ups when short on time.

name: Single-arm dumbbell row
rationale: Thick mid-back, one side at a time — posture insurance for hours hunched into wind.
cues: Knee and hand on bench, flat back
Row to the hip, not the armpit
Squeeze, lower slow, no torso twist

name: TRX row
rationale: Scales to any level by foot position; plank and pull at once.
cues: Body rigid as a board
Pull handles to lower ribs
Feet forward = harder
swap_note: Rack-mounted straps tip unless you go fully flat — using the chest-supported dumbbell row until strong enough to do this flat.

name: TRX push-up / dips off bench
rationale: Pressing volume without more dumbbell juggling.
cues: TRX push-up: handles low, body plank-rigid
Bench dips: shoulders down away from ears
Stop 2 reps shy of failure

name: Curls + band pull-aparts
rationale: Direct arm work (you said you want to see the fruits) plus rear-delt posture reps.
cues: Curl strict — no swing
Pull-aparts: squeeze shoulder blades, band to chest
Superset them, 2 rounds, done

name: Pallof press
rationale: Anti-rotation — the core skill of running with a pack in a crosswind.
cues: Band anchored at the rack, stand side-on
Press out, resist the twist, pause 2 s
Half-kneeling version = harder than it looks

name: Dead bug
rationale: Trunk control with a protected spine — perfect on tired days.
cues: Low back gently pressed to floor throughout
Opposite arm and leg reach long
Slow exhale each rep

name: Bird dog
rationale: Part of McGill’s Big 3 — spine stability with zero cost.
cues: Reach long, not high
Hips stay level — imagine a mug of tea on your back
Pause 3 s each rep

name: Side plank
rationale: Lateral trunk endurance — camber and pack-lean resistance.
cues: Elbow under shoulder, body one line
Hips high
Progress: top leg raised or feet on bench

name: Hanging knee raise
rationale: Grip endurance + lower abs from your pull-up bar.
cues: Hang tall, no swing
Knees to chest with a posterior pelvic tilt
Lower slow

name: Chest-supported dumbbell row
rationale: Stand-in for the TRX row while the rack-mounted straps aren't safe to load — same horizontal pull, chest braced so nothing can tip.
cues: Chest flat on the incline bench
Pull dumbbells to your lower ribs
Lower under control, no swing
swap_note: Back to the TRX row once you can load it fully flat without the rack tipping.

name: Cat–cow
rationale: Gentle segmental spine motion to open the session — wakes the lumbar and thoracic spine through their full range with zero load.
cues: On all fours, wrists under shoulders, knees under hips
Exhale and round the spine to the ceiling; inhale and let it sag
Move slowly, led by the breath — never force the end range

name: Kneeling hip-flexor stretch
rationale: Runners live in hip flexion, and a tight front hip drags the pelvis into tilt and dumps the load on the low back. Open it up.
cues: Half-kneeling, back knee on a pad, front foot flat
Tuck the tailbone under first, then glide the hips forward
Squeeze the glute on the kneeling side — feel it in the front hip, not the low back

name: Open-book rotation
rationale: Rotation the mid-back should own so the lumbar spine does not have to. Frees the trunk for pack carriage and an honest running posture.
cues: Side-lying, knees stacked and bent, arms stretched out in front
Open the top arm across to the floor behind you, eyes following the hand
Keep the knees pinned together — the twist comes from the ribcage

name: Glute bridge
rationale: Teaches the glutes to extend the hip so the low back can stop doing their job — the cornerstone of a back that lasts.
cues: On your back, feet flat, heels drawn in close to your hips
Drive through the heels and squeeze the glutes to lift
Ribs down, no arching — the motion is all hips, not low back
swap_note: Single-leg glute bridge once the two-leg version feels easy.

name: Supine hamstring stretch
rationale: Tight hamstrings tug the pelvis under and rob the hip hinge; lengthen them lying down so the low back stays neutral throughout.
cues: On your back, loop a strap or towel around one foot
Raise the leg until you feel a gentle stretch, knee softly straight
Keep the opposite leg down and the low back quiet
